topics.title: Rome: from republic to empire
topics.dek: Five centuries of a republic, and the decade that ended it

slides.h: A city that threw out its king
slides.p: Tradition dates the Roman Republic to 509 BC, when the last king was expelled and power passed to elected magistrates. The founding fear was one man ruling alone; the whole design was built to prevent it, which makes how it ended the point of the story.

slides.h: Power split so nobody kept it
slides.p: Two consuls served one year and could veto each other. The Senate of former magistrates advised, controlled money and held real authority. Assemblies of citizens passed laws and elected officials; tribunes could veto on behalf of the plebeians. In an emergency a dictator served six months, then stepped down.

slides.h: Conquest made the republic rich and unstable
slides.p: By 146 BC Rome had destroyed Carthage and taken Greece. Plunder and slaves poured in; wealthy senators bought up farmland into vast estates worked by slaves, and the small farmers who had filled the legions drifted landless into the city. The army and the land became the political questions.

slides.h: Reformers, and the first political murders
slides.p: In 133 BC the tribune Tiberius Gracchus pushed land redistribution and was clubbed to death by senators; his brother Gaius followed a decade later. The norm against killing political opponents, once broken, never came back. Each generation's violence set the floor for the next.

items: Gaius Gracchus dies in street fighting
Sulla marches his army on Rome
Sulla's proscriptions: enemies' names posted, killed

slides.p: Around 107 BC Gaius Marius opened the legions to the landless poor, who served for pay and for the land their general could win them at retirement. Their loyalty followed the man, not the state. Sulla, Pompey and Caesar each commanded armies that were, in practice, theirs.

Julius Caesar, back from conquering Gaul, was ordered to give up his command and face prosecution. Instead he led a legion across the Rubicon, the stream marking the limit of his province, into Italy. Civil war followed; Pompey lost; Caesar became dictator for life in 44 BC and was stabbed to death a month later.

v.q: Alea iacta est — the die is cast.
v.by: attributed to Caesar at the Rubicon, 10 January 49 BC

slides.h: Augustus keeps the forms, takes the power
slides.p: Caesar's heir Octavian defeated Antony and Cleopatra at Actium in 31 BC. In 27 BC he 'restored the Republic' to the Senate, which in return named him Augustus and left him command of the armies and the provinces that had them. Consuls were still elected. They just no longer decided anything.

The Republic lasted almost five hundred years; the slide from political murder to private armies to one-man rule took about a century. Its institutions, the two consuls, the vetoes, the term limits, were copied by the American founders, who had read how it ended and tried to design around it.

items: One man holds all the offices (27 BC)

quiz.q: The Roman Republic was designed above all to prevent…
quiz.why: Two consuls with mutual vetoes, one-year terms and a time-limited dictatorship were all guards against a king.

quiz.q: Marius's army reform mattered because soldiers became loyal to…
a: Their general, who paid them and promised land
quiz.why: A private army is a political weapon. Sulla, Pompey and Caesar each used one.

quiz.q: Caesar crossing the Rubicon in 49 BC was significant because…
a: It meant bringing an army into Italy, which was treason
It was the border with Gaul
quiz.why: Generals had to leave their armies at the provincial border. Crossing it under arms began the civil war.

take: 509 BC to 27 BC: a republic built to prevent one-man rule, undone in about a century.
Broken norms, then private armies, then a general in the city.
Augustus kept every institution and emptied them of power.
src: Crisis of the Roman Republic — Wikipedia

topics.title: The Silk Road
topics.dek: Not one road, not mostly silk: fifteen centuries of exchange

slides.p: The German geographer Ferdinand von Richthofen coined 'Seidenstraße' for routes that linked China to the Mediterranean from about 130 BC, when the Han dynasty opened trade westward, to 1453, when the Ottomans took Constantinople. No one travelled the whole length; goods passed hand to hand.

items: Zhang Qian's mission west for the Han

slides.p: From Chang'an (Xi'an) along the Gansu corridor, around the Taklamakan desert by the north or south oasis towns, over the Pamirs to Samarkand and Bukhara, through Persia to Baghdad, and on to Antioch and the Mediterranean ports. A parallel maritime route ran from south China through India to the Red Sea.

slides.h: What moved east, what moved west
slides.p: Westward: silk, paper, porcelain, tea, gunpowder, the compass. Eastward: horses, glass, wool, gold and silver, grapes, and crops like alfalfa. Most trade was in short hops between neighbouring markets; a bolt of silk might change hands a dozen times before Rome.

Buddhism went from India into Central Asia and China along the trade routes; the cave temples at Dunhuang are its milestones. Islam spread east along the same roads after the 7th century. Nestorian Christianity reached Tang China. Mathematics, astronomy and medicine moved in both directions.

slides.h: The oasis cities got rich on the traffic
slides.p: Samarkand, Bukhara, Merv and Kashgar lived by caravanserais, markets and tolls. Sogdian merchants from around Samarkand were the great middlemen for centuries; their language was the lingua franca of the route. Empires that controlled the chokepoints, Persia especially, taxed everything.

items: largest city in the world c. 1150

slides.h: Paper and gunpowder changed the West
slides.p: Papermaking reached the Islamic world after 751 (Chinese prisoners taken at Talas, according to tradition) and Europe by the 12th century, making books cheap enough for the printing press to matter. Gunpowder arrived in the 13th century and remade warfare and castles within two hundred years.

items: Paper credited to Cai Lun in Han China

slides.h: The Mongol peace, and the plague
slides.p: In the 13th century the Mongol Empire unified the route from Korea to Hungary; travel was safer than ever and Marco Polo's generation went to the Yuan court. The same open roads carried the Black Death westward in the 1340s, killing a third or more of Europe. Connection cut both ways.

b: a third of Europe dead by 1351

slides.h: Why it faded, and why it's back
slides.p: After 1453 the Ottomans controlled the western end, the Mongol order was gone, and Portuguese ships found the way round Africa in 1498; the sea was cheaper. Today China's 'Belt and Road' borrows the name for ports, railways and loans across the same geography, with the same arguments about who profits.

items: Mongol unity fractures; tolls and bandits rise
1498: Vasco da Gama reaches India by sea

quiz.q: The term 'Silk Road' was coined…
quiz.why: Ferdinand von Richthofen named it long after the routes had declined. People who used it had no single name for it.

quiz.q: Most goods on the Silk Road travelled…
a: The full length with one merchant
In short hops between neighbouring markets
quiz.why: Almost nobody went end to end. Silk changed hands many times, rising in price at each stop.

quiz.q: Besides goods, the routes carried…
a: Religions, technologies and, in the 1340s, plague
quiz.why: Buddhism, Islam, paper and gunpowder moved along them; so did the Black Death under the Mongol peace.

take: A network of hops, not one road, from about 130 BC to 1453.
Silk and paper went west; horses and glass went east; religions and plague went both ways.
It declined when the sea route round Africa made it unnecessary.

topics.title: The Black Death
topics.dek: Four years that killed a third of Europe and rearranged everything after

slides.p: Yersinia pestis lives in rodents and the fleas that bite them. Bubonic plague causes swollen lymph nodes (buboes), fever and death in half of cases untreated; the pneumonic form spreads person to person by cough and kills nearly everyone. Antibiotics treat it today; in 1347 nobody knew what it was.

slides.h: From the steppe to Sicily in a few years
slides.p: The outbreak probably began in Central Asia in the 1330s and travelled the Mongol trade routes. In 1346 it reached the Genoese port of Caffa on the Black Sea; ships carried it to Messina in Sicily in October 1347, and from there to every port in the Mediterranean within months.

Estimates for Europe run from a third to a half of the population between 1347 and 1351: roughly 25 to 50 million people. Cities were worst hit; Florence may have lost 60 percent. The Middle East and North Africa suffered comparably. World population didn't recover for about two centuries.

Physicians blamed bad air (miasma) and the planets; the Church called it divine punishment. Flagellants whipped themselves through towns. Jewish communities were accused of poisoning wells and massacred in dozens of cities despite papal condemnation. Quarantine, from the Venetian for forty days, was the one idea that worked.

With a third of the workers gone, survivors could demand wages; English rural wages roughly doubled over the following decades. Lords tried to freeze pay by law (the Statute of Labourers, 1351) and failed. Peasants moved to better terms; the bond of serfdom loosened across Western Europe.

Pressure between wage laws and labor shortages fed the Jacquerie in France (1358) and the English Peasants' Revolt (1381). The Church lost clergy at high rates and credibility with them; the questions survivors asked about suffering and authority fed into the Reformation a century and a half later.

The 1347 wave was the first of many: plague returned every decade or two for three centuries. The Great Plague of London in 1665 killed perhaps a quarter of the city. A third pandemic began in China in 1855 and carried the disease worldwide; the bacterium was identified in Hong Kong in 1894.

Historians argue about how much the plague caused: higher wages, land for the taking, a shift from labor to capital, more meat in the diet, the Renaissance's patrons. It is still with us: a few thousand cases a year worldwide, treatable with antibiotics if caught early, including a handful in the American West.

items: Wages up, serfdom weakened in the West
Still endemic in rodents; ~1,000–3,000 cases a year

quiz.q: The Black Death was caused by…
a: A bacterium carried by fleas on rodents
quiz.why: Yersinia pestis, identified in 1894. Bubonic plague came from flea bites; pneumonic plague passed by cough.

quiz.q: Between 1347 and 1351, Europe lost roughly…
quiz.why: Estimates are 25 to 50 million dead. Some cities lost more than half.

quiz.q: One lasting economic effect of the plague was…
a: Rising wages and weaker serfdom in the West
No change; populations recovered within a decade
quiz.why: Scarce labor could bargain. Wage caps like England's Statute of Labourers failed to hold.

take: A flea-borne bacterium that moved along trade routes: Caffa 1346, Messina 1347, all of Europe by 1351.
A third to a half of Europe died; the dead left scarce, better-paid labor behind.
Quarantine was the one idea that worked; the disease is still here and now treatable.

topics.title: The printing press
topics.dek: How a goldsmith's machine in Mainz made the modern world argue

slides.h: Before 1450, a book was a year of someone's life
slides.p: Manuscripts were copied by hand, mostly in monasteries, on parchment made from animal skins. A Bible took a scribe about a year and cost as much as a farm. Europe had perhaps a few hundred thousand books in total. Knowledge moved at the pace of the copyist.

v.c: for one scribe to copy one Bible

slides.h: Printing wasn't new; movable metal type was
slides.p: China printed from carved wood blocks from the 9th century and Bi Sheng made ceramic movable type around 1040; Korea cast metal type by 1377. Chinese script's thousands of characters limited the payoff. Gutenberg's innovation, around 1440 in Mainz, was a system: cast metal type, oil-based ink and a screw press.

items: Diamond Sutra, earliest dated printed book (China)

slides.p: A hand mould cast identical letters from a lead-tin-antimony alloy, thousands an hour once set up. Letters were composed into pages, inked with a sticky oil-based ink that stuck to metal, and pressed onto paper with a screw press adapted from wine making. Every part existed; the combination didn't.

Gutenberg's Bible ran to about 180 copies. By 1500, presses in some 270 European cities had printed an estimated 20 million books, more than all the scribes of the previous thousand years. By 1600, as many as 200 million. The price of a book fell by perhaps two-thirds within decades.

In 1517 Martin Luther nailed up ninety-five academic theses in Latin. Printers translated and reprinted them; within weeks they were across Germany, within months across Europe. Luther wrote in German for the press, and pamphlets were a third of German printing by the 1520s. The Reformation was a media event.

items: Everything else in German, same years

slides.h: Science needs the same text in many hands
slides.p: Printed books let scholars in different cities check the same diagrams and tables, spot errors and build on each other. Vesalius's anatomy (1543) and Copernicus's heliocentric model (1543) depended on exact, repeatable illustrations. Standardised maps, star tables and mathematics followed.

Cheap texts in the vernacular gave people reasons to read, and printers standardised spelling and grammar as they went: printing fixed English, French and German into their modern forms. Reading shared news and books in the same language is part of how people came to think of themselves as nations.

Authorities answered with licensing, indexes of banned books (the Catholic Index from 1559) and the first copyright laws (England, 1710). Every later information technology, the telegraph, radio, the internet, has replayed the cycle: cheap copies, a flood of pamphlets, panic about misinformation, new rules.

items: A new normal, more literate than before

quiz.q: Gutenberg's key contribution was…
a: Combining cast metal type, oil ink and a screw press into one system
quiz.why: Block printing and movable type existed in Asia centuries earlier. The workable, scalable combination was his.

quiz.q: By 1500, roughly how many books had European presses produced?
quiz.why: About 20 million in fifty years, more than all the manuscripts of the previous millennium.

quiz.q: The press mattered to the Reformation because…
a: Pamphlets spread his arguments across Europe in months
quiz.why: Printers reprinted and translated his theses within weeks. He wrote for the press in German.

take: Around 1440, Gutenberg made a system of cast type, oil ink and a screw press.
Twenty million books by 1500; the Reformation and modern science rode on them.
Cheap copies brought literacy, standard languages, and censorship: a pattern every new medium repeats.

topics.title: The Renaissance
topics.dek: Florence, the Medici, perspective and the recovery of the ancient world

slides.p: 'Rinascita' was used by the painter-biographer Vasari in 1550 for the revival of ancient Greek and Roman art and learning in Italy. Historians date it from roughly the 1300s to the 1600s, beginning in the city-states of northern Italy, above all Florence, and spreading north across the Alps after 1500.

items: Fall of Constantinople; Greek scholars flee west
Sack of Rome; the High Renaissance ends

slides.p: Wool and banking made it rich; the Medici family's bank funded popes and kings, and the family spent on artists and scholars for prestige and piety. It was a republic of guilds with a competitive civic pride; cathedral doors, domes and chapels were commissions fought over publicly.

Petrarch and his followers hunted monastic libraries for lost Latin texts and, after 1400, learned Greek. Humanism put the study of language, history, poetry and ethics (the 'humanities') at the center of education, with human dignity and achievement as worthy subjects, not a turn away from religion.

Around 1415 Brunelleschi demonstrated linear perspective: parallel lines converge at a vanishing point, so a flat panel can show measurable depth. Alberti wrote the rules down in 1435. Masaccio's Trinity fresco (c. 1427) is the first great painting built on them. Space became a subject.

items: Horizon line at the viewer's eye level
Objects shrink in proportion to distance

slides.h: The dome nobody knew how to build
slides.p: Florence's cathedral had stood for a century with a 140-foot hole in its roof; no timber centering could span it. Brunelleschi won the 1418 competition with a double-shell dome of self-supporting brick rings laid in herringbone, built without scaffolding from the ground. Finished in 1436, it is still the largest brick dome.

The High Renaissance, roughly 1495 to 1527, compressed the three into one generation in Florence and Rome: Leonardo's Last Supper (1498) and Mona Lisa, Michelangelo's David (1504) and Sistine ceiling (1512), Raphael's School of Athens (1511). Patrons were popes and dukes; the artist became a famous individual.

rows: David, Sistine ceiling, St Peter's dome

slides.p: The Medici were bankers who became rulers: Cosimo ran Florence from 1434 without holding office, Lorenzo 'the Magnificent' from 1469. Two became popes (Leo X, Clement VII) and two became queens of France. Their patronage bought legitimacy; their fall in 1494 and return in 1512 track the city's politics.

items: Giovanni de' Medici becomes Pope Leo X
Medici become Grand Dukes of Tuscany

slides.h: North of the Alps, and what it left
slides.p: Printing carried humanism north: Erasmus, Thomas More, Dürer's engravings, the Flemish painters' oil technique (which the Italians adopted). The Renaissance left the idea that antiquity could be recovered and improved on, the artist as genius, perspective in every image since, and the humanities on every curriculum.

items: The individual artist, signed and celebrated
Oil paint from the north, printing everywhere

quiz.q: Renaissance humanism was mainly a return to…
a: The study of ancient Greek and Roman texts and the humanities
quiz.why: Humanists recovered classical sources and put language, history and ethics at the center of learning; most were devout.

quiz.q: Brunelleschi is remembered for…
a: Linear perspective and the Florence cathedral dome
quiz.why: He demonstrated perspective around 1415 and built the largest brick dome in the world without centering, 1420–36.

quiz.q: The Medici's power in Florence rested on…
a: Banking wealth and patronage, often without formal office
quiz.why: Cosimo ruled from behind the scenes from 1434. Later Medici became popes, queens and finally dukes.

take: Roughly 1300–1600, Florence first: wool and banking money, civic competition, recovered classics.
Perspective (1415) and the dome (1436) made art measurable; the artist became a name.
Printing carried it north and fixed its ideas into Western education.

topics.title: The French Revolution
topics.dek: From a bankrupt king to the guillotine to Napoleon in ten years

slides.h: A kingdom that couldn't pay its bills
slides.p: By 1788 France spent about half its revenue on interest, much of it from helping the Americans beat Britain. Nobles and clergy paid almost no tax; the commoners (the Third Estate) paid nearly all of it. Bad harvests in 1788 doubled the price of bread. Louis XVI called the Estates-General for the first time since 1614.

The Third Estate declared itself a National Assembly in June and swore not to disband until France had a constitution. On July 14 a Paris crowd stormed the Bastille. In August the Assembly abolished feudal privileges and declared the Rights of Man. In October women marched on Versailles and brought the king to Paris.

items: Declaration of the Rights of Man

slides.h: Liberty, equality, and the question of the king
slides.p: A constitutional monarchy was written in 1791. Louis tried to flee abroad in June and was caught at Varennes, which destroyed trust. War with Austria and Prussia began in April 1792; defeats and fear of invasion radicalised Paris. In August the crowd stormed the Tuileries and the monarchy was suspended.

The new National Convention tried Louis XVI for treason and voted for death by a narrow margin. He was guillotined on 21 January 1793; Marie Antoinette followed in October. Every monarchy in Europe joined the war against France. The revolution could no longer be undone by compromise.

v.c: Louis XVI executed; Europe's crowns declare war

slides.p: Facing invasion, civil war in the Vendée and famine, the Committee of Public Safety under Robespierre ruled by emergency decree from 1793 to 1794. About 17,000 were executed after trial and tens of thousands more died in prison or the provinces. It ended when the Convention turned on Robespierre in July 1794 and guillotined him.

items: Died in prison or without trial

slides.p: Feudal dues, noble titles and church tithes were abolished; church lands were sold; the metric system was created (1795); law was made uniform; careers opened to talent; Jews were emancipated (1791). Slavery was abolished in the colonies in 1794 (Napoleon restored it in 1802).

items: Equality before the law; privileges gone

slides.p: Five years of unstable Directory government, coups and war fatigue ended when a young general, Napoleon Bonaparte, seized power on 18 Brumaire (9 November 1799). He kept the revolution's legal equality and codified it (the Civil Code, 1804), crowned himself emperor the same year, and exported code and conquest across Europe.

The revolution gave politics its vocabulary: left and right (from where deputies sat), nationalism, ideology, the citizen-soldier, human rights as a declaration. It showed a people could remove a king and that a revolution could devour its own. Every revolution since has been argued through its example.

quiz.q: The immediate trigger for calling the Estates-General in 1789 was…
a: Royal bankruptcy and the need for new taxes
quiz.why: Debt from war, a privileged class that paid little tax and bad harvests forced Louis XVI to summon it.

quiz.q: The Terror ended when…
a: The Convention arrested and executed Robespierre in July 1794
quiz.why: The Thermidorian reaction turned the emergency machinery on its chief architect.

quiz.q: The political terms 'left' and 'right' come from…
a: Where deputies sat in the revolutionary assemblies
quiz.why: Supporters of the king sat to the president's right, radicals to the left.

take: Bankruptcy and privilege brought the Estates-General; 1789 moved from oath to Bastille to rights in four months.
War radicalised it: the republic in 1792, the king's execution in 1793, the Terror in 1793–94.
It ended in Napoleon, but left equality before the law, the metric system and the words left and right.
src: Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen — Yale Avalon Project

topics.title: The Industrial Revolution
topics.dek: Coal, cotton and steam: how Britain changed how everyone lives

slides.p: For most of history, income per person barely moved; a peasant in 1700 lived roughly as one in the year 1000. From about 1760 in Britain, output per person began rising and never stopped. Almost every chart of human material life bends upward at this point.

Cheap coal near the surface; high wages that made labor-saving machines worth building; a market of 10 million people under one law; colonies and the Atlantic trade supplying cotton and buying cloth; secure property, patents, banks; and a culture of tinkering engineers. No one factor was enough; Britain had all of them.

Spinning was the bottleneck: it took several spinners to feed one weaver. Hargreaves's spinning jenny (1764), Arkwright's water frame (1769) and Crompton's mule (1779) multiplied one worker's output by hundreds. Cloth prices collapsed; Britain's cotton exports grew about a hundredfold between 1760 and 1830.

items: Arkwright's water frame; Watt's engine patent

slides.h: Steam makes the factory free of the river
slides.p: Newcomen's engines pumped mines from 1712; James Watt's separate condenser (1769) made them efficient, and his rotary engine (1781) could drive machinery anywhere coal could be carted. Factories left the fast streams for the cities. Coal output rose from about 3 million tons in 1700 to 65 million by 1850.

Smelting iron with coke instead of charcoal (Darby, 1709) and Cort's puddling process (1784) made iron cheap. Put it under a steam engine on rails: Stephenson's Rocket (1829) and the Liverpool–Manchester line (1830) started a boom; Britain had 6,000 miles of track by 1850. Goods, people and news moved at thirty miles an hour.

Manchester grew from about 25,000 people in 1770 to 300,000 by 1850. Twelve- to fourteen-hour days, child labor from age six, cholera in the slums; average height actually fell for a generation. Factory Acts from 1833 limited children's hours and sent inspectors; the ten-hour day came in 1847.

Belgium, France and the German states industrialised from the 1830s, the United States with New England textiles and then railroads, Japan after 1868. A second wave (steel, electricity, chemicals, oil) ran from about 1870. Industrial power became military power: the gap between industrialised and not decided the age of empires.

Most people now live in cities, work for wages, measure time by clocks, and expect their children to live better than they did; none of that was true in 1750. The same engines began loading carbon into the air, which is the bill now arriving. It is the most consequential change in human life since farming.

v.c: share of people living in cities, Britain

quiz.q: The first industry transformed by machines in Britain was…
quiz.why: The spinning jenny, water frame and mule multiplied one spinner's output by hundreds from the 1760s.

quiz.q: James Watt's improvements to the steam engine mattered because…
a: They made engines efficient enough to drive factories anywhere coal could be brought
quiz.why: Newcomen's engines existed from 1712; Watt's separate condenser and rotary motion freed factories from rivers.

quiz.q: Average heights fell for a generation in early industrial Britain because…
a: Of a change in diet fashion
Urban slums, long hours and disease outpaced wage gains
quiz.why: Living standards for workers lagged output for decades; Factory and sanitation acts came from the 1830s.

take: From about 1760 in Britain, output per person began rising and never stopped.
Cotton, then steam, iron and rail; coal underneath all of it.
Cities, wage work and rising expectations are its legacy; so is the carbon.
src: Our World in Data: Economic growth

topics.title: How the First World War started
topics.dek: An assassination, five weeks of telegrams and a war nobody could stop

slides.p: By 1914 the great powers were locked into alliances: Germany, Austria-Hungary and Italy in the Triple Alliance; France, Russia and Britain in the Triple Entente. Military plans assumed the next war would be short and that mobilising first would win it. A quarrel between any two could pull in all six.

Archduke Franz Ferdinand, heir to Austria-Hungary, was shot in Sarajevo by Gavrilo Princip, a Bosnian Serb nationalist linked to a secret society in Serbia. Vienna saw its chance to crush Serbia, the magnet for its restless South Slavs, and asked Berlin for backing.

Austria's 48-hour ultimatum of 23 July was written to be refused. Serbia accepted nearly all of it; Vienna declared war anyway on 28 July and shelled Belgrade. Russia, Serbia's protector, began to mobilise. Once Russia moved, German plans required an immediate strike at France through Belgium.

Mobilising millions by rail took days of fixed schedules. Germany's Schlieffen Plan had one option: knock out France in six weeks via Belgium, then turn east before slow Russia was ready. There was no plan for a war against Russia alone. When the Kaiser asked for one on 1 August, he was told it did not exist.

items: Germany must beat France first: the only plan
The route is through neutral Belgium
Five declarations of war in eight days

slides.h: Why they thought it would be short
slides.p: Recent wars (1866, 1870) had been decided in weeks. Generals believed offence and morale would overwhelm defence. Few had absorbed what machine guns, magazine rifles and quick-firing artillery had done in the American Civil War, the Boer War and the Russo-Japanese War. 'Home by Christmas' was sincere.

The German advance was stopped on the Marne in September 1914, twenty miles from Paris. Both sides then tried to outflank each other north to the sea and failed. By November a line of trenches ran 440 miles from Switzerland to the Channel. It moved less than ten miles either way in the next three years.

v.c: of trenches, Switzerland to the sea, by November 1914

slides.p: Verdun (1916) cost about 700,000 casualties; the Somme about a million, with 57,000 British casualties on the first day alone. By 1918 some 9 to 10 million soldiers and perhaps 7 million civilians were dead. Four empires, the German, Austro-Hungarian, Russian and Ottoman, did not survive it.

slides.h: The lesson historians still argue over
slides.p: Was it German ambition, Austrian recklessness, Russian mobilisation, alliance systems, rigid plans, or sleepwalking leaders who all thought someone else would back down? The record supports pieces of each. What's not in dispute: the machinery of alliances and mobilisation turned a Balkan murder into a world war in five weeks.

quiz.q: Germany invaded neutral Belgium in August 1914 because…
a: Its only war plan required defeating France quickly by that route
quiz.why: The Schlieffen Plan assumed a two-front war and struck France first through Belgium, which brought Britain in.

quiz.q: The war's first weeks ended with…
a: A stalemate and 440 miles of trenches
quiz.why: The Marne stopped the German advance; the race to the sea produced a line that barely moved for three years.

quiz.q: How many empires collapsed as a result of the war?
quiz.why: German, Austro-Hungarian, Russian and Ottoman. The map of Europe and the Middle East was redrawn.

take: Alliances plus mobilisation timetables turned Sarajevo into a world war in five weeks.
Everyone planned for a short war; the machine gun and the trench made it four years.
Nine to ten million soldiers dead, four empires gone, and the seeds of 1939.
src: Imperial War Museums: How the First World War began

topics.title: The Cold War in ten cards
topics.dek: Forty-five years of rivalry that never became a direct war, and nearly did

slides.h: Allies who didn't trust each other
slides.p: The United States and the Soviet Union defeated Germany together and divided Europe between them at Yalta and Potsdam in 1945. Within two years the partnership was over: Stalin installed communist governments across Eastern Europe, and Washington decided to contain Soviet power wherever it pushed.

items: NATO founded; Soviet atomic bomb; China goes communist

slides.p: George Kennan's 1947 analysis argued Soviet expansion could be held in check by patient counter-pressure. The Truman Doctrine funded Greece and Turkey; the Marshall Plan put about $13 billion (roughly $150 billion today) into rebuilding Western Europe, which also made it a market and a bulwark.

slides.h: Berlin: the airlift and the Wall
slides.p: In 1948 Stalin cut road and rail access to West Berlin, an island inside the Soviet zone. For eleven months Allied planes flew in everything, landing every few minutes, until he gave up. In 1961 East Germany built a wall through the city to stop its people leaving; 140 or more died trying to cross it before 1989.

v.c: flights in the Berlin Airlift, June 1948 – May 1949

slides.h: The bomb, and the balance of terror
slides.p: The Soviets tested an atomic bomb in 1949, both sides had hydrogen bombs by the mid-1950s, and intercontinental missiles by the 1960s. Mutual assured destruction meant neither side could strike without being destroyed. The arsenals peaked at about 70,000 warheads in 1986.

The superpowers fought through others: Korea (1950–53, about 3 million dead), Vietnam (U.S. combat 1965–73), Afghanistan after the Soviet invasion of 1979, plus coups and civil wars from Guatemala and Iran to Angola and Nicaragua. The Cold War was cold in Europe and very hot elsewhere.

U.S. spy planes found Soviet nuclear missiles in Cuba. Kennedy imposed a naval 'quarantine'; Soviet ships approached it. On 27 October a U-2 was shot down and a Soviet submarine officer refused to fire a nuclear torpedo. Khrushchev withdrew for a public U.S. pledge not to invade Cuba and a secret one on missiles in Turkey.

items: 24 Oct: Soviet ships stop at the line

slides.p: Sputnik (1957) and Gagarin (1961) shocked America into the Moon programme. The 1970s brought arms treaties (SALT I, 1972), Nixon in China (1972) and the Helsinki Accords (1975), then renewed tension after Afghanistan and Reagan's buildup. The economic race was being lost by a Soviet system that couldn't produce consumer goods.

b: a budget drained by arms and Afghanistan

slides.p: Mikhail Gorbachev took over in 1985 and tried reform: glasnost (openness), perestroika (restructuring), arms cuts, withdrawal from Afghanistan, and a refusal to use force to prop up Eastern European regimes. In 1989 they fell one after another; the Berlin Wall opened on 9 November. The Soviet Union dissolved on 26 December 1991.

items: INF Treaty scraps a missile class

quiz.q: 'Containment' meant…
a: Holding Soviet expansion in check with steady counter-pressure
quiz.why: Kennan's 1947 doctrine shaped U.S. policy for four decades: aid, alliances and proxy wars rather than direct war.

quiz.q: The Cuban Missile Crisis ended with…
a: A Soviet withdrawal in exchange for U.S. pledges, one public and one secret
quiz.why: Khrushchev pulled the missiles out; the U.S. promised not to invade Cuba and quietly removed missiles from Turkey.

quiz.q: The Berlin Wall came down in…
quiz.why: 9 November 1989, after Gorbachev declined to back the East German regime with force. The USSR dissolved two years later.

take: 1947–1991: containment, alliances and proxy wars, held in check by mutual destruction.
Berlin, Korea, Cuba 1962 and Afghanistan were the flashpoints.
It ended when a Soviet leader chose reform over force and the system could not survive openness.
src: U.S. State Department, Office of the Historian: Kennan and containment

topics.title: The Space Race
topics.dek: From Sputnik's beep to Apollo 11 in twelve years

slides.p: Sputnik 1 was a 184-pound polished sphere that broadcast a radio pulse anyone could tune in. The rocket that launched it could also carry a warhead across an ocean, which is what alarmed Washington. Within a year the U.S. had passed the National Defense Education Act and created NASA.

First satellite, first animal, first man (Yuri Gagarin, 1961), first woman (Valentina Tereshkova, 1963), first spacewalk (Alexei Leonov, 1965), first probe to hit the Moon and photograph its far side. Their chief designer, Sergei Korolev, was a state secret until he died in 1966.

Six weeks after Gagarin and a month after the Bay of Pigs, Kennedy asked Congress to commit to landing a man on the Moon 'before this decade is out'. The U.S. had fifteen minutes of human spaceflight experience. It was a bet that a long, hard goal would play to American industrial strength.

v.q: We choose to go to the Moon in this decade and do the other things, not because they are easy, but because they are hard.
v.by: John F. Kennedy, Rice University, 12 September 1962

slides.p: Mercury (1961–63) proved a person could survive orbit. Gemini (1965–66) practised the hard parts: rendezvous, docking, spacewalks, two-week flights. Apollo was the Moon programme itself, built around the Saturn V, a 363-foot rocket that remains the most powerful ever successfully flown until 2022.

slides.h: The cost, in money and lives
slides.p: Apollo cost about $25 billion by 1973, roughly $250 billion today; at the peak NASA took over 4 percent of the federal budget and employed 400,000 people through contractors. Three astronauts died in the Apollo 1 cabin fire in January 1967; the Soviets lost Vladimir Komarov in Soyuz 1 three months later.

slides.h: Apollo 8: around the Moon at Christmas
slides.p: In December 1968 Borman, Lovell and Anders became the first humans to leave Earth orbit and circle the Moon, ten times. Anders's photograph 'Earthrise' and the crew's Christmas Eve broadcast reached a quarter of the world's population. The Soviets' giant N1 rocket, meanwhile, failed on all four launches.

v.c: from Earth; Apollo 8 was the first crew to make the trip

slides.p: Eagle landed in the Sea of Tranquility with about 25 seconds of fuel margin, after Armstrong flew past a boulder field by hand. Six hours later he stepped onto the surface; Aldrin followed. They spent two and a half hours outside, collected 47 pounds of rock and were home on 24 July. About 600 million people watched.

items: 16 Jul: launch from Kennedy Space Center

slides.p: Six landings and twelve people walked on the Moon by December 1972; nobody has since. The programme left weather and communications satellites, integrated circuits pushed to maturity, 842 pounds of Moon rock, and in 1975 a handshake in orbit (Apollo-Soyuz). The new race, to return and to Mars, has more players.

items: Artemis I flies uncrewed around the Moon

quiz.q: Sputnik alarmed the United States mainly because…
a: The rocket that launched it could carry a warhead across an ocean
It was larger than any U.S. satellite
quiz.why: The satellite was a radio beacon. The R-7 launcher was an intercontinental missile.

quiz.q: Gemini's purpose was to…
quiz.why: Everything Apollo needed except the Moon itself was rehearsed in Gemini's ten crewed flights in 1965–66.

quiz.q: How many people have walked on the Moon?
quiz.why: Twelve, on six Apollo landings from 1969 to 1972. Twenty-four flew to the Moon; none has returned since.

take: Sputnik 1957, Gagarin 1961, Kennedy's pledge 1961, Apollo 11 1969.
Mercury proved orbit, Gemini practised the manoeuvres, Apollo went.
Twelve moonwalkers by 1972, none since; satellites and chips were the lasting payoff.
